content.thinking:
I need to organize Manish's concerns from both the WhatsApp messages and the PDF document into a comprehensive list, structured by source and theme to make sure I capture everything completely.

Starting with the WhatsApp conversation from July 30th: he opens by saying he's being direct because it's more useful than politeness. He identifies three style issues across the posts — first, he uses too many hedges and pre-apologies ("I want to be fair," "I want to be careful") when he should just make claims and acknowledge costs directly. Second, all his examples feature male voices, which doesn't represent his actual audience. Third, he mentions that the onboarding call didn't capture his real identity and defining character, so he's providing a separate document with his core pillars and unique story as the actual spine. Then he goes through each post: Post 1 needs the receptionist detail emphasized (moved twice in two months) while dropping the $3M reference entirely and vaguifying other parts. Post 2 should be cut entirely because he dislikes the World Cup analogy approach.

Post 3 contradicts how he actually operates — the longer document covers it better. Post 4 has one of his best ideas with two excellent lines, but the payroll paragraph needs to go completely since it reads harsh and he'd never publish it that way; the graphic is too generic. Post 5 should be killed because it might discourage potential vendors. Post 6 is true but the voice is flat and doesn't sound like him — the best line is buried and should lead instead. Post 7 is the right direction but needs specificity like Hormozi's work; it's currently two degrees off generic. He wants to explain why knowing numbers matters and what a damaged-shipment reaction reveals — the real insight is that they plan and price for decisions that won't work out, which is their actual business model. Post 8 contains a factual error about him that he cares deeply about correcting: he hasn't bought or handed out AI tools and deliberately held back from doing so.

He uses AI heavily himself daily at a deep level and is personally all in, but organizationally cautious as a deliberate strategy. Nearly every AI post out there is either evangelism or skepticism, and that's what makes his actual stance so unique and contrarian. Post 9 has the right underlying content but the hook doesn't sound like him.

Looking at the PDF feedback now — this is the strategy layer beyond the individual post comments. The audience read is validated as correct, resellers aren't on LinkedIn, brand principals are, brand acquisition over lead gen is right, and the four target roles are accurate. He's emphasizing this is a proposal not an instruction, and he'd rather be corrected now than six weeks in since I do this for a living and he doesn't. Now examining the spine and the three pillars of concern.

The real issue is that the three pillars read as separate subjects rather than one cohesive argument, which is why the drafts feel like ten disconnected posts instead of a unified body of work. The proposed spine is "Software did not eat my world. Trust runs it" — and it connects across credit as trust priced, hiring as trust built inward, vendor negotiation as trust currency, handshakes as trust made physical, and succession as trust transferred across generations. This reaches because LinkedIn business content is written by SaaS founders, agency owners, VCs, and consultants whose product is software or content itself, but the people who actually live in his world don't write, and the people who write have never lived it. That intersection is empty, which is exactly where he sits.

The arc for page three is that his greatest strength doesn't scale — one of him against 250 of them. The company survives without him but won't grow, so the eighteen-month story becomes building an institution that holds judgment and trust without him, which he's uncertain he can pull off. The real concern is ego: a feed built entirely on his own judgment can sour quickly and repel the exact reader he wants to reach. The protection isn't false modesty in the copy, which reads worse than the boast anyway — it's keeping the arc itself in the work. The three pillars shift here: the operator becomes a judgment engine, the market splits between judgment and corrections, and the inside TLM dissolves since facilities and country counts are just table stakes that every distributor claims.

There are four engines driving this, with the long game and judgment making up about seventy percent of the value, corrections handling most of the rest, and machinery only appearing when it clears a certain threshold. The long game is the biggest engine and it's something his current strategy misses entirely. The second generation question is the real strategic point — every brand wonders about family-owned distributors: Is it dependent on the founder's relationships? Does it survive the handover? Does the son have systems or just inheritance? Nobody asks directly, but everybody asks it. He's answering this in public in real time, which is an underserved subject. The rule is never to post about his father or the family itself, only about what changes when a business stops running on one person's relationships. An old company carries thirty years of accumulated decisions that nobody re-reads, which is a generous and more accurate frame than putting him above the company he inherited. He's built almost everything without outside work experience, which means he's reinvented some wheels and things took longer, but every process is explicable by the person running it rather than borrowed from a consultant — though this can read as insular to a vendor executive, so he counterweights it by taking exploratory meetings constantly to learn and avoid being isolated.

Now I'm thinking about building something that outlasts him, which means the senior layer needs to carry strategy, not just execution. He's thinking about this with an early forties horizon, which is harder than standard advice admits. HR is a good example — six years ago there was no structure, now it's one of his most demanding relationships and the teams he works with most closely. New tech and AI go there first. He's proudest of and hardest on the same things, which is the line to keep. The guardrail is avoiding anything that reads as public disappointment in a named team, since HR leadership reads LinkedIn, so the broad arc and timeline are public but the precise mechanics and live org decisions stay internal.

He does around 600 interviews a year, compared to Chesky's 300, because his role as hiring manager assesses fit for specific vacancies, which is legitimate but a different question from what he's thinking about. "Culture fit" language masks what we're actually selecting for — comfort with ambiguity, building systems rather than maintaining them, willingness to be shaped by the role. The receptionist becomes the proof point of how we operate: we don't hire for slots, we hire people and figure out what they're built for, which means most of my leadership team never applied for the jobs they ended up in. That said, we get it wrong sometimes, and that honesty matters for credibility.

On brand selection, I'm thinking through the cycle preference — products that move like boxes over drawn-out enterprise deals — and the vendor equation of quality plus ambition plus real support infrastructure. There's a margin and volume test too: too niche and you can't scale, too crowded and margins disappear. The posture is aggressive with larger brands, never accepting disadvantageous terms, willing to walk away entirely.

Fragmentation is the real killer for brands — two well-backed distributors outperform six competing on price alone. I've seen both models play out in identical regions and categories, and that's the most valuable insight to share with brand principals. But the guardrail is firm: publish the principle and pattern, never name the brands, because one of those models is a live counterparty and a public critique ends the relationship fast.

On credit assessment, I'm looking at content that's one degree off generic, signals that stay unexplained. The numbers-without-checking test reveals whether they're running the business or it's running them — better predictor of repayment than any filing. A damaged shipment shows whether they raise it before you do, cheapest behavioral test at scale. The real insight gets nearly discarded: the value in pricing the calls that don't land.

Now moving into the corrections engine — naming the advice, showing the world as it actually is, then stating the corrected rule. The AI position is the one he cares most about. On firing fast, the correction isn't that he's trapped; he built a different mechanism using reassignment before removal, but the identifying details and tenure history have to come out. Digital-first means leading with the buried line.

For the machinery engine, I'm being sparse and selective. The five-degree rule is the filter: anyone can search what a letter of credit is, so a post answering what a machine answers better is worse than nothing. It only earns space with a decision rule, a real cost, a failure mode, or a number from their own book.

I'm now organizing the specifics: the facts to correct, permanent exclusions, and two open items around cadence and measurement. Time to write this up clearly for Ansh in a scannable format.

But first I should flag the meta-level concerns — that the call didn't capture his narrative arc, the drafts read as disconnected pieces rather than a cohesive body of work, the ego risk, and his preference for correction over agreement. Then I'll write it all out. No tools needed, just a complete answer that matches what he asked for.

Here is everything he raised, from both sources.

## Source 1 — WhatsApp, 30 July, 20:05–21:13

**How he framed it:** *"Being direct because that's more useful to you than being polite."*

**What he liked**
- Post 10 (automating my own job) — "the best thing in the batch by a distance"
- Posts 7 (credit) and 4 (approval chain) — "direction is right"

**Three style concerns**

| | Concern | His words |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Hedging** | "I want to be fair to the tools", "I want to be careful there", "I am not saying that to sound modest" — *"Let's make the claim, let's acknowledge the cost, but do we really have to apologize / pre-apologize?"* |
| 2 | **Every voice is male** | *"all the anecdotes / examples in the 10 posts are male voices — 'who he will be having a problem with at 11pm'"* |
| 3 | **Slop** | "Here is the part that nobody puts on a slide" — *"the kind of line I'd never write"* |

**A fourth, bigger one he stated in passing:** *"It tells my unique story. My defining character. **Perhaps the call did not capture it.**"* — he felt the onboarding call missed who he actually is.

**Post by post**

1. **Salesperson** — the strongest fact isn't his age, it's that he joined as the **front desk receptionist** and was moved twice in two months. Drop the $3M entirely. Getting the employee's consent himself.
2. **Arsenal** — cut it. *"I really hate 'I saw the World Cup and here's how it relates to my work' kind of posts. It's so forced."*
3. **Nine things before firing** — *"the opposite of how we actually work."*
4. **Ten weeks** — the idea is one of the best found, two lines excellent. But cut the payroll paragraph **completely, doesn't publish in any form**. Reads as him walking in and finding a mess — *"reads a bit harsh."* And **the graphic is generic**.
5. **Lightwave** — kill it. *"might discourage potential vendors from partnering with us."*
6. **Handshake** — *"the voice is flat. Doesn't sound like me."* Best line is buried; lead with it, cut most of the rest.
7. **Credit** — *"Hormozi is sooo specific. This post is just 2 degrees off generic."* Why does knowing his numbers matter? What does the damaged-shipment reaction actually tell you? The real insight is pricing for the decisions that don't work out — *"that's the business model."*
8. **AI** — **factually wrong about him**, and *"the correction I care most about."* He hasn't bought tools and handed them out; he's deliberately held back. Personally all in, organisationally cautious. *"the most unique / contrarian thing I've got."*
9. **Everything I touch gets 10x better** — content underneath is right, *"the hook is not me."*

---

## Source 2 — the 11-page PDF

**He opened by validating the strategy:** the audience read is right, resellers aren't on LinkedIn, brand principals are, brand acquisition over lead gen is correct, the four target roles are accurate. *"That was the hard part of the thinking and you got it right."* And: *"This is a proposal, not an instruction… If you think there is a better through-line, argue it. I would rather be corrected now than six weeks in."*

**§1 — The core structural concern.** Three pillars are *"three subjects rather than one argument, which is part of why the drafts read as ten separate posts instead of a body of work."* His proposed spine: **"Software did not eat my world. Trust runs it."** Credit is trust priced. Hiring is trust built inward. Vendor negotiation is trust as currency. The handshake is trust made physical. Succession is trust transferred across a generation.

**Why it reaches:** business content here is written by SaaS founders, agency owners, VCs and consultants. *"The people who live my world do not write, and the people who write have never lived my world. That intersection is empty."*

**§1 also — the ego risk.** A feed built on his judgement *"can curdle fast."* The protection is **not modesty in the copy** — *"which reads worse than the boast"* — it's keeping the arc in the work: he's trying to make himself unnecessary at the thing he's best at.

**§3 — The long game, "the engine your current strategy misses entirely"**
- **He is 36. The business is 30. His father built it.** The second-generation transition is the question every brand asks about a family-owned distributor and nobody asks out loud. **Rule: never a post about his father or the family** — always about what changes when a business stops running on one person's relationships.
- **Nothing here was borrowed** — almost no work experience outside TLM. Cost: reinvented wheels. Benefit: no process exists because a consultant recommended it. Risk to manage: reads insular to a vendor exec, so the counterweight (constant exploratory meetings to learn, not to deal) belongs in the same post.
- **HR is the vehicle** for making judgement institutional. *"The team I am proudest of and the team I am hardest on, and those are the same sentence."* Guardrail: nothing that reads as public disappointment in a named team — **his HR leadership reads LinkedIn.**

**§4 — Judgement**
- **600 interviews a year**, Chesky stopped at 300. Guardrail: *"cannot read as I do not trust my managers."*
- **Six things he reads** in the first two minutes, plus the half that matters — instinct that can't be explained can't be taught, and anything untaught stops at him.
- **"A home for a certain kind of person"** — and a specific warning: *"culture fit as a phrase now carries baggage… reads as a euphemism for hiring people who resemble the people already there."* Describe the traits instead. Also: no more than one post in ten leaning on somebody else's framework.
- **The receptionist is the flagship.** *"His age and the money are stories about him. The receptionist is a story about how TLM works, which is the only kind that helps us."* Non-negotiable: no revenue figure, no salary — *"that post is a poaching brief."*
- **Brand selection philosophy** — cycle first, vendor equation, margin/volume test, posture. Philosophy publishes, live pipeline doesn't.
- **Fragmentation kills brands.** Firm guardrail: don't name them — *"one of those models is running at a live counterparty of ours, and a public post critical of a vendor relationship is the fastest way to end it."*

**§6 — The five degree rule.** *"A post that answers a question a machine answers better is worse than no post."* A machinery post earns its place only with a decision rule, a real cost, a failure mode, or a number from their own book.

**§7 — Eight factual corrections.** CEO not MD (his father is MD and Group Chairman) · 30 years is the business, not him · 250 not 240 · pick one country count · 600 interviews, *"do not round it upward — a reader divides by working days in fifteen seconds"* · the 60% and 3x figures need verifying · promotions and the 100-times credit claim need checking · he'll verify the "everyone moved internally" claim himself.

**§8 — Seven permanent exclusions.** Compliance/tax/regulatory/legal/entity financials however anonymised — *"Operator judgement, yes. Operator confessions, no."* · named vendors in critical framing · identifiable employees without consent · salaries and revenue attribution · pipeline brands and forward category bets · internal timelines and live decisions · **any claim they deliberately placed a brand into a market** — *"several of our strongest partnerships came to us because of presence we already had, and I will not dress that up as strategy I executed."*

His reason for making these standing rules: *"At this cadence I will not be reading every draft with fresh eyes by week six, so the line has to hold without me."*

**§9 — Two things he wants argued**
- **Cadence:** 4 a week, not 8. *"Tell me if you disagree on the volume and why, because that part is your area more than mine."*
- **Measurement:** *"impressions are not a number I will make a decision on."* Proposes brand-side inbound from the four roles, logged, with a number by day 90.

---

**The pattern worth noticing:** almost none of this is taste. It's a client who thinks in guardrails, who caught a factual error about himself, who is protecting a live vendor relationship and his own HR team from our copy, and who explicitly asked to be argued with twice.

**Meeting: 4pm UAE / 5:30 IST. Here's what you need.**

## The WhatsApp message, in 30 seconds

He read all 10 posts and went post-by-post. Opened with *"being direct because that's more useful to you than being polite."* Verdict: **kill 2** (Arsenal, Lightwave), **1 is factually wrong about him** (the AI post), **1 is the best thing in the batch** (automating his own job), rest need work. Three style notes: stop hedging, stop apologising, and every single example in the batch was a male voice.

## The PDF, in 30 seconds

It's not a complaint document — it's the strategy he thinks we should be running. He wrote 11 pages because **he felt the onboarding call didn't get who he is**. It opens by telling us we got the hard part right (brand acquisition, not lead gen), then says our three pillars are *"three subjects rather than one argument"* and proposes a single spine: **"Software did not eat my world. Trust runs it."** Then four content engines, his actual material, 8 factual corrections, 7 permanent no-go rules, and 2 things he wants us to argue with him about.

---

# The 5 that must be resolved in the room

### 1. His spine replaces our structure — say yes fast and clearly
He's proposing we drop the 3 pillars for one argument: everything he does is trust. Credit is trust priced. Hiring is trust built inward. The handshake is trust made physical. Succession is trust across a generation.

**He's right, and it's better than ours.** Say so in the first two minutes. *"You've solved the thing I hadn't — the pillars were three subjects, not one argument. We're rebuilding the deck around trust."* Don't defend the old version.

### 2. Why he had to write 11 pages
Read between the lines: *"Perhaps the call did not capture it."* A client spending a full day writing your strategy for you is either very invested or losing confidence. **Address it head-on, don't wait for him to raise it.** *"You shouldn't have had to write this. The call didn't get deep enough and that's on me — here's how the next one is structured."*

### 3. We got his AI position backwards
Our post said he bought tools and the team ignored them. **The truth is the opposite** — he's deliberately held back from rolling it out to 250 people because the guardrails don't exist yet, while using it himself daily at real depth. He called this *"the correction I care most about"* and *"the most contrarian thing I've got."*

This is the one that costs trust, because we invented a position for him. Own it plainly. It's already rewritten in the new batch.

### 4. Cadence — he asked you to argue
He wants **4 a week, not 8**: *"Tell me if you disagree on the volume and why, because that part is your area more than mine."*

**Agree with him.** His feed is at 2.5 posts a *month* — 4 a week is already a 7x jump, and the bar he's describing can't hold at 8. Say you'll revisit at day 60. He'll respect the agreement more than a fight.

### 5. Measurement — he won't accept impressions
*"Impressions are not a number I will make a decision on."* He wants one leading indicator agreed **before week one ships**: brand-side inbound conversations from the four target roles, logged, with a number by day 90.

**Take it, and add one thing:** inbound will lag the first month, so also log profile views filtered to those roles — that gives you something visible by day 30 instead of 90 days of silence.

---

## Quick confirms to get before you hang up

- **The receptionist post is blocked on his consent** — he said he's getting it. It's the strongest post in the batch.
- **"Nobody on my leadership team applied for the job they have"** — he said he'd verify it's literally true. Best line we have.
- **The brand list and philosophy PDF never reached us** — WhatsApp stripped them. Ask him to email.

## One thing to be careful about

His 7 permanent exclusions are a compliance regime, not preferences. The sharpest one: **never name a vendor critically** — one of the models he describes is running at a live counterparty, and *"a public post critical of a vendor relationship is the fastest way to end it."* Also, his HR leadership reads LinkedIn, so nothing that reads as disappointment in that team.

**Everything from both documents is already implemented in the new drafts** — https://app.thesnowball.agency/preview-linkedin/manish-week1-v14. Lead the call with the strategy, not the posts.

=== PHILOSOPHY PDF: 2 pages ===
--- p1 ---
 
 
Brand Onboarding Philosophy 
1. The Cycle. First question – how does the brand move? “Enterprise brands” have 
long deal-cycles, consultants, POCs, and people-dependent relationships. “Box 
brands” is the business we prefer to be in 9 times out of 10.  
 
That doesn’t mean we only deal in the big, established names that sell 
themselves. We’re happy to introduce new or misrepresented brands, conduct 
trainings, onboard resellers, run marketing – but once that’s done – at the end, 
we want to deal in quick deal cycles. This is how our current portfolio is for the 
most part, and we aim to onboard to our team's actual capability.  
2. Vendor Quality + Ambition + Support = Ideal. Mimosa, Cudy, Ruijie... nobody 
knew these names when we started. We built them. But we build as the 
committed partner with real distribution protection, vendor support, vendor 
marketing investment, training, and RMA support. If the brand is thinking long-
term, and ready to invest, we're happy to be onboard. 
  
3. Geography is the key to some brands. The same brand might be over-
represented in Dubai with 4 distributors, but invisible in West Africa or Central 
Asia. This is an opportunity. We’ve onboarded an A-tier brand like Acer for West 
Africa distribution (we operate 3 entities in West Africa – Mali, Burkina Faso, and 
Cameroon). UGreen is another A-tier brand we’re in conversation with thanks to 
our West Africa reach (warehouses + offices + real stock and people on the 
ground). Similarly, we’ve onboarded Synology for Central Asia thanks to our 
partner coverage, even though we don’t have a branch office there. 
 
4. Margin + Volume. Brands in too small a niche don’t work since the volumes are 
too small. Similarly, brands in too crowded a segment (e.g. SSDs) typically don’t 
work either, since the margins are too small. This is very subjective and a broad 
direction rather than a fixed rule. 
 
5. Consideration: we are happy to aggressively reach out to larger brands and 
make a case for ourselves, but we never want to be onboarded at a 
disadvantage. We want brands to see the value we’re offering and bring us on 
strategically, happily. Never reluctantly. 
 
6. Future-Focused Verticals. The two verticals I would bank on for the future are 
(a) self-hosted AI hardware, and (b) Robotics.  
 
The former fits into most of the brand philosophy I have outlined here, but there 
is no clear leader here, but the industry is still rapidly evolving. Open claw on a 
--- p2 ---
 
 
Mac mini was considered the gold standard three months ago for self-hosted AI 
hardware, until Nvidia announced its own AI mini PCs, and that itself got 
upstaged by AMD’s AI mini PC announcements just a few weeks later. We'd like 
to build relationships and maybe enter this space at this point in time, but it's 
hard to say who will be the top players once this initial gold rush settles and 
pricing begins to stabilize. I haven't been able to identify or name AI hardware 
brands at this point in time (in my sheet), but it is an important vertical for the 
future. 
 
Robotics is the only industry that I'm willing to invest in early and build an entirely 
new team around. It is contrary to every point of my onboarding philosophy, but I 
consider the opportunity here too large to ignore. It's worth building an entirely 
new business unit and a new way of working in order to be one of the first movers 
in this space. I believe that industrial robots will fundamentally alter the course 
of our timelines, and we don't want to be watching from the sidelines when they 
explode in popularity. I have named several robotics companies in my sheet.

==============================================================================
POST 1 — receptionist-flagship   [tweet card]   AWAITING CONSENT
==============================================================================

Our best salesperson joined us as the front desk receptionist

we moved him twice in his first 2 months...

Most companies hire for a slot and then measure the person against the slot. If the fit is poor they decide the hire was a mistake.

We do it the other way round. We hire the person, slowly and carefully, and then keep working out what they are actually for. That is why our interviews take so long, and it is why the seat stays negotiable long after somebody has taken it.

He was not a hiring error that got corrected. He was read correctly at the front desk, and read correctly again 2 months later.

We move people between roles and teams far more often than a business our size normally would. In most organisations that would be disruptive, and here it has become the thing that grows us. The alternative is watching a capable person fail in the wrong seat and calling it a performance problem.

Nobody on my leadership team applied for the job they have.

I should say plainly that we get this wrong sometimes, and anyone who has ever hired anyone will already know that. The wins outnumber the misses by a wide margin, which is the only claim I will make.

The seat is the easiest thing in the building to change. The person is not.

==============================================================================
POST 2 — ai-personally-all-in   [whiteboard]   READY
==============================================================================

I use AI every single day, at real depth

and I have deliberately not rolled it out to 250 people...

Those two things get read as a contradiction. They are the same decision.

Personally I am maximalist about it, because it handles the preparation that sits in front of most of my week. That is the briefing, the history, the numbers and the first draft of whatever I am walking into.

Organisationally I have held back, and it is not caution for its own sake. The standardisation and the guardrails I would want before putting this in front of 250 people do not exist yet at the standard I need. Unmanaged variance across an organisation is a risk I am not willing to distribute.

A tool that makes 1 person faster is a gift, but the same tool unmanaged across 250 people produces 250 slightly different standards of work. You have no way of telling which is which until a customer finds out for you.

So I am running it at depth on myself first, which is also the only honest way to know what the guardrails need to be.

Almost every AI post on this platform is either evangelism or scepticism. I do not think it is either. It is a sequencing question, and most companies are answering it in the wrong order.

==============================================================================
POST 3 — six-hundred-interviews   [tweet card]   READY
==============================================================================

Brian Chesky interviewed the first 300 people who joined Airbnb, then had to stop

we are 250 people and I am still in almost every hire...

That works out at close to 600 interviews a year, 2 or 3 on most working days, and I delegate nearly everything else in this company.

People assume this is a control problem. It is the opposite, and the reason is structural rather than personal.

A hiring manager is assessing whether somebody fits a vacancy. That is a completely legitimate question and it is not the one I am asking. I am assessing the person against the whole company, and I am the only one in the building who sees every seat at once.

There are 2 other reasons I have never handed this over:

- a candidate reveals different things when the person across the table owns the consequences
- culture drifts at the hiring gate long before it drifts anywhere else, and 20 slightly wrong hires leave you a different company with the same logo

This is deliberately expensive, and that is the point. Nobody spends this much of a calendar on interviews as a shortcut.

It is the single largest recurring commitment I have, and I protect it ahead of almost everything else on the schedule.

==============================================================================
POST 4 — old-decisions   [structured graphic (new)]   READY
==============================================================================

It took 10 weeks to approve 1 day of leave

and nobody in the building could tell me why...

There was no meeting where somebody chose a 10 week approval chain. It accumulated. A form here and an extra signature there, and every one of them was sensible on the day it was added.

That is not a failure, and I want to be accurate about it rather than flattering to myself. Any business that survives 30 years accumulates decisions nobody goes back and re-reads. Ours had 30 years of them, which is what 30 years of surviving looks like from the inside.

The sentence I kept hearing is the one that should worry any operator: this is how we have always done it.

An old company is not old technology. It is old decisions that nobody revisited, because everybody assumed somebody once had a reason.

So the test I use now is 1 question. If I cannot find the person who decided it, it probably does not need to exist.

That approval chain is 1 step today. Same outcome, same risk, same protection, and about 10 weeks of somebody's patience given back.

The decisions worth keeping survive being asked about. That is the whole test, and almost nothing else in a company gets audited this way.

==============================================================================
POST 5 — credit-mechanism   [whiteboard]   READY
==============================================================================

One of our customers went from 1 shop to 13

the signals we read on him are not on any filing...

Across much of Africa the formal filings and bureau scores are thin, so the industry defaults to selling somebody only what they can pay for that morning. They stay exactly the size they are, and so does the distributor. That second half is the part people leave out.

We read a different set of things instead, and each one is doing specific work:

- whether they know their own numbers without going to check. That tells me whether they are running the business or the business is running them, and it predicts repayment better than any filing I have ever been handed.

- what they do when a shipment turns up damaged. Whether they raise it before we do is the cheapest test available of how somebody behaves when something goes wrong at scale.

- how they talk about their last shipment. People who are close to their own operation talk about it in specifics, and people who are not talk about it in summaries.

None of that is generosity, and here is the part that makes it a business rather than a gamble. We price for the calls that do not land, which is exactly what lets us keep making them.

Everyone else in this market treats a loss as a mistake. We treat it as a line in the model, and that difference is why the same story has now repeated many times across our book.

Credit is a growth strategy that happens to sit inside the finance department.

==============================================================================
POST 6 — market-not-real   [photo]   READY
==============================================================================

A market is not real to me until somebody from my team has stood in it

that rule has not changed in 6 years...

I sell into 56 countries, and a large share of my leads still start with a handshake.

Not because the tools do not work. We run email, we do SEO, we are building better outbound than we have ever had, and I fund all of it.

None of it replaces the 90 seconds where a country head walks past our stand and sees a product they have only read about. In that time they decide whether we are serious people.

Most digital-first advice is written by people selling into 1 market, in 1 language, where the institutions do the trusting on your behalf. In the markets I sell into, the buyer wants to see who they are going to have a problem with at 11 at night.

The uncomfortable part is that I cannot tell you which handshake will turn into anything, and I still have to fund all of them.

So I keep buying the software, and I am not cancelling the flights.

==============================================================================
POST 7 — what-i-read   [structured graphic (new)]   READY
==============================================================================

People call it instinct

it is a few thousand conversations compressed into the first 2 minutes...

Instinct posts are usually insufferable, because they present the gut as something mystical that the writer happens to possess. The credible version is the opposite of that, and it is just a mechanism running fast.

Here is what I am actually reading:

- where they put responsibility in the sentence. "We shipped late and here is what I did" is a different person from "the warehouse let us down".

- specificity. People who did the work remember details and people who supervised it remember summaries, and the difference shows inside 90 seconds.

- what they ask about. Curiosity about the business rather than only about the package.

- stamina. Anyone is sharp for 5 minutes, and I want to see what is still there at 20.

- whether they have ever done something unglamorous well. That predicts more than any qualification on the page.

- how they react to being told they may be offered a different role than the one they applied for. That single reaction tells me whether they will do well somewhere that moves people around.

Now the half that actually matters. Instinct that cannot be explained cannot be taught, and anything that cannot be taught stops at me.

Most of the last few years has gone into getting the core team to read people the same way. They now do, and that is the only reason 600 interviews a year has not become a bottleneck sitting on my desk.

==============================================================================
POST 8 — reassignment-before-removal   [whiteboard]   READY
==============================================================================

Hire slow, fire fast was written for companies where removal is cheap

in my world it is not, and that changed the mechanism rather than the speed...

The advice assumes you correct a hiring mistake by taking the person out. That works when taking somebody out is quick and cheap. Here it is neither, because labour process is not optional, relationships walk out of the door with the person, and 250 people watch how every exit is handled.

The obvious conclusion is that I am trapped into keeping people longer than I should. That is not what happened.

Because the hire was made against the person rather than against the vacancy, my first question when performance dips is not whether the person is wrong. It is whether the seat is.

So we reassign before we remove. It is slower, it looks softer than it actually is, and over 6 years it has produced far more wins than misses.

The version of this that fails is the one where reassignment is a polite holding pattern before an exit everybody can see coming. If the move is real, the person knows inside a week, because the work changes.

Fire fast is good advice for a company that can afford to be wrong quickly. I would rather build one that is wrong slowly and then fixes it properly.

==============================================================================
POST 9 — outlast-myself   [photo]   READY
==============================================================================

The company I want does not have me sitting in the middle of it

so I am trying to make myself unnecessary at the thing I am best at...

There is 1 of me and 250 of them. The business survives without me. It does not yet grow without me, and those are very different sentences.

So I am building a senior layer that can carry strategy rather than only execution, and I have given myself a horizon in my early forties to get there.

It is harder than the standard advice admits, and not for the reasons people assume. Signing serious money against growth that has not happened yet feels different inside a family business. Anybody who has done both will know what I mean. I am doing it anyway, with more discomfort than I expected to feel.

The vehicle for most of this is HR, which is not where people expect it to sit.

6 years ago we had no HR structure at all. Today it is one of the teams I work with most closely and one of the most demanding relationships I have. New technology and new processes go there first, because anything that survives contact with 250 people will survive contact with a customer.

It is the team I am proudest of and the team I am hardest on, and those are the same sentence.

If judgement is ever going to live in the institution instead of in me, that is the team it has to live in first.

==============================================================================
POST 10 — automate-my-own-job   [photo]   READY, HIS FAVOURITE
==============================================================================

I have spent 1 year trying to automate my own job

6 things are still stopping me...

1. A sales call that opens in English and closes in Hindi, and I have tested this one myself more than once. The accent is not the problem any more, because the models handle that fine, but the language switch is what breaks them. My customer moves into Hindi halfway through a negotiation, sometimes into a dialect of it, and the whole thing falls over.

2. Deciding who gets credit, which I have come to think is the most intangible judgement in my entire business. There are no filings to pull, no bureau score and no audited accounts, so the signals are entirely our own. What I listen for is how somebody talks about their last shipment, and whether they raise the damage before I ask about it. I do not believe a model reads any of that off a conversation with a seller, and I have not seen one come close.

3. Reading a room, because a large share of my leads still begin with somebody walking past our stand and deciding in 90 seconds whether we are serious people. Nobody has shown me how you automate 90 seconds.

4. Telling me which brand is actually hungry, since I can pull a list of 500 brands available to distribute in an afternoon. Available and ambitious are not the same word, and I have paid real money to learn where that line sits.

5. Rebuilding trust with a supplier we let down, which is 40 small decisions taken over 8 months. No prompt I have tried makes 40 small decisions over 8 months.

6. Knowing a good person is about to leave, because by the time it shows up in their work they have already decided and I am the last one to find out.

Now the part I did not expect, and it is the reason I would not go back.

It already does the 4 hours of preparation sitting in front of every one of those 6 moments. The briefing, the history, the numbers and the first draft of what I want to say are handled before I walk in.

That is most of my week, and I did not lose a single thing I wanted to keep.

Everybody keeps telling me that AI will take the judgement and leave me the admin, but in my business it has done the exact opposite. I will take that trade every time.

# Talking points

## Open with this (first 60 seconds)

> "Your document is better than mine. The three pillars were three subjects, not one argument — you're right, and 'trust runs it' is the spine. We're rebuilding around it. And you shouldn't have had to write 11 pages; the call didn't go deep enough, and that's on me."

Lead with the strategy. Don't open with the posts.

## The one to own properly

**The AI post was factually wrong about you.** We wrote that you bought tools and the team ignored them. The truth is the opposite. Say it plainly, don't over-apologise, then move: *"It's rewritten. Personally maximalist, organisationally conservative — and you're right that it's the most contrarian thing you own."*

## Where you agree (say yes fast, it buys credibility)

| His ask | Your answer |

# The permanent, strategic items

Post fixes are done and disposable. **These are the ones that outlive this batch** — decide them once and they govern everything.

## 1. The spine — one argument, not three subjects

**"Software did not eat my world. Trust runs it."**

This is the biggest thing in his document. Our three pillars were three *topics*; his is one *thesis* that everything folds into — credit is trust priced, hiring is trust built inward, vendor negotiation is trust as currency, the handshake is trust made physical, succession is trust transferred across a generation.

**Why it's strategically right, not just nicer:** he identified an empty market position. Business content on LinkedIn is written by SaaS founders, VCs, agency owners and consultants — people whose product is software or the content itself. *"The people who live my world do not write, and the people who write have never lived my world."* That intersection is genuinely unoccupied.

**Decide in the meeting:** we adopt it, and the deck gets rebuilt around it.

## 2. The four engines and their weighting

Replaces the pillars permanently. **Long game + judgement ≈ 70%** of everything. Corrections engine takes most of the rest. Machinery runs rarely.

This matters because it's a *standing allocation*, not a batch plan. Every future week gets measured against it.

## 3. The five degree rule

His quality bar, and it should become ours across all clients:

> *"Anyone can ask a search engine what a letter of credit is, and a post that answers a question a machine answers better is worse than no post."*

A post earns its place only if it carries something an operator paid to learn: **a decision rule, a real cost, a failure mode, or a number from their own book.** That's the sharpest content test I've heard from a client.

## 4. The seven permanent exclusions — treat as compliance, not preference

His reason is the important part: *"At this cadence I will not be reading every draft with fresh eyes by week six, so the line has to hold without me."*

**He is delegating trust to us.** Two are commercially live, not stylistic:
- **Never name a vendor critically** — one of the models he describes runs at a live counterparty. *"The fastest way to end it."*
- **The brand list never publishes.** 590 rows of live pipeline — "in discussion via intermediary", "CIS signed, UAE pending" — plus robotics as a forward bet. All excluded by his own §8.

The philosophy document, by contrast, **does** publish — minus the named brands and the future verticals.

## 5. The ego guardrail

Subtle and easy to get wrong. A feed built on his own judgement *"can curdle fast, and that costs us the exact reader we want."*

**His fix is not modesty** — he explicitly says modesty *"reads worse than the boast."* The protection is that **the arc stays in the work**: he is trying to make himself unnecessary at the thing he's best at. Keep that tension in and it reads as someone building something; take it out and it reads as someone admiring himself.

This directly overrides the "no self-deprecation" rule you gave me last week. The reconciliation: **no confession, but keep the unfinished ambition visible.**

## 6. Cadence as a standing decision

4 a week, not 8 — and the *reason* is permanent: the bar he's describing can't be held at 8 without falling back on the machinery posts he wants used sparingly. **Quality bar sets volume, not the reverse.** Revisit at day 60.

## 7. The measurement contract

*"Impressions are not a number I will make a decision on."* Agree the leading indicator **before week one ships**: brand-side inbound from the four target roles, logged, number by day 90 — plus profile views filtered to those roles, so there's a visible signal by day 30 instead of 90 days of silence.

## 8. The relationship point

He wrote 11 pages because *"perhaps the call did not capture it."* He also said twice that he wants to be argued with: *"I would rather be corrected now than six weeks in."*

**The permanent change is how we run discovery.** The onboarding call went wide across his business and never got to his defining character. That's the process fix, and saying so unprompted is worth more than any post correction.

# Manish Keshwani — everything we know

## 1. The person

- **36 years old.** CEO of TLM Group. His father is Managing Director and Group Chairman.
- The **business is 30 years old, he is not**. His father built it. He is the second generation.
  This distinction is a standing correction: never attribute 30 years of operating to him.
- Based in **Dubai**. Windows user. Uses an authenticator app, not SMS OTP.
- **Almost no work experience outside TLM.** Nearly every process at TLM was built in the last 5 or
  6 years, from the problem upward.
- Married with family (unconfirmed detail, do not publish).
- Colours he likes, asked directly: **red, purple, pink**. Strongest pull is **purple** — "big fan",
  knows it signified royalty in Rome. "Not afraid to shy away from bright colours."
- Reads, but not exhaustively. Knows "parts of" Blitzscaling. Engages seriously with ideas when
  they are put to him.

  forms with Claude rather than paying DocuSign.

## 2. Character, as he describes himself

- Runs the business on **judgement and trust**, and knows that is a scaling problem.
- Interviews **close to 600 people a year**, 2 to 3 on most working days, across 250 staff and
  5 entities. Delegates nearly everything else. Has never handed this over.
- Deliberately expensive habits are the point: "nobody spends this much of a calendar on
  interviews as a shortcut".
- Self-aware about ego risk in content: a feed built on his own judgement "can curdle fast".
  His fix is not modesty — "modesty reads worse than the boast" — but keeping the unfinished
  ambition visible.
- Direct. Opened his feedback with "being direct because that's more useful to you than being
  polite". Asked twice to be argued with: "I would rather be corrected now than six weeks in."
- **Delegates once convinced.** On the 31 Jul call: "I'll also sort of allow you to do your job…
  I'll not try to step on it. If it's a flag only from compliance or security, I'll let you know."

## 3. The business

- **TLM Group.** Tech and logistics distribution. **56 countries. 250 people. 5 entities.**
  18 brands. Website tlminternational.com.
- Entities include **3 in West Africa**: Mali, Burkina Faso, Cameroon. Warehouses, offices, real
  stock and people on the ground.
- **T4** — logistics arm, launched Oct 2025. DG (dangerous goods) facilities.
- **Lightwave** — their own house brand. Doing $20M, he believes it should do $100M.
  **DO NOT PUBLISH.** He killed this post: may discourage vendors from partnering.
- Best salesperson **joined as the front desk receptionist**, moved twice inside 2 months.
  The receptionist detail is the story; the revenue figure is not publishable.
- **Nobody on his leadership team applied for the job they have.** He is verifying this is literally
  true before it publishes.
- **6 years ago TLM had no HR structure at all.** Today HR is the team he works with most closely,
  the most demanding relationship he has, and where new tech and AI experiments go first.
  "The team I am proudest of and the team I am hardest on, and those are the same sentence."
- Inherited a **10 week approval chain for 1 day of leave**. Now 1 step. His test: "if I cannot
  find the person who decided it, it probably does not need to exist."
- Credit is a growth strategy, not a risk function. One customer went from 1 shop to 13.
  Mechanism: they **price for the calls that do not land**, which is what lets them keep making them.

## 4. Brand onboarding philosophy (his own document, publishable minus the names)

1. **The cycle first.** Prefers "box brands" over "enterprise brands" 9 times out of 10. Long deal
   cycles, consultants, POCs and people-dependent relationships are the thing he avoids. Happy to
   build unknown brands with training, reseller onboarding and marketing, as long as the end state
   is quick deal cycles. Onboards to what the team can actually execute.
2. **Quality + ambition + support = ideal.** Built Mimosa, Cudy, Ruijie from nothing. Requires
   distribution protection, vendor support, marketing investment, training, working RMA.
3. **Geography is the key.** A brand can be over-represented in Dubai with 4 distributors and
   invisible in West Africa or Central Asia. That gap is the opening. Won Acer for West Africa and
   Synology for Central Asia this way. **This is the strongest publishable insight in the document.**
4. **Margin + volume.** Too niche fails on volume, too crowded fails on margin. A direction, not a
   fixed rule, but it kills more candidates than anything else.
5. **Posture.** Pitches larger brands aggressively, never onboards at a disadvantage. "We want
   brands to bring us on strategically, happily. Never reluctantly."
6. **Future verticals: self-hosted AI hardware and robotics.** Robotics is the one bet he would
   build an entirely new business unit and team around, contrary to every other point in his
   philosophy. **NOT PUBLISHABLE — forward-looking category bet.**

Also his: **fragmentation kills brands.** A brand appointing 2 distributors and backing them
properly beats one appointing 6 who compete on price. He has watched both models run in the same
region, same category, same time. Publish the principle, never the brands — one model is running
at a live counterparty.

## 5. The brand master list — INTERNAL ONLY, PERMANENTLY

Covered by his own permanent exclusion. **Never appears in content, in any form, ever.**

## 6. THE PIVOT — agreed on the 2026-07-31 call

The single most important strategic fact about this account.

**The problem Ansh named:** content built on TLM's own stories is limited by the context we hold,
requires continuous input from Manish, and is a **corporate account, not a creator account**.
Manish cannot sustain 11 pages of feedback a week and should not have to.

**The new positioning: creator, not corporate.**
> "Being a creator, all you have to do is provide value to your audience, and your audience will
> never be your customer."

he wants to hire senior leadership over 1 to 3 years, weighted **80% modern talent / 20% executives**
— negotiation, sales, marketing, founder's office, AI integration, GTM. A creator with an audience
gets a better candidate pool than a job post, plus easier side projects. Brand acquisition continues
in parallel through DMs, not through the feed.

**The content formula, agreed line by line on the call:**
1. **Objective brag** to earn the right to be heard. Hormozi's "I sold 2 $100M companies", never
   "I am the best at this". Manish drew this distinction himself and it is the rule.
2. **A humbling re-hook** that contradicts or qualifies the brag.
3. **Then real value**, usually a listicle. "Anybody would want to learn the 18 things believed by
   a person running a $200M company."

**Evergreen material is explicitly authorised.** Books, Paul Graham, a16z, Naval, Reid Hoffman,
Zero to One — packaged and topped with *his* opinion. "Everybody wants to know what the guy running
a $200M company thinks about this book."

**Hard nos from the call:**
- **Not a guru profile.** No coaching energy. "Extremely intellectual and not towards guru."
- **Not an AI creator.** Do not make AI the topic.
- **Never fake him.** No online/offline mismatch.
- The profile must read as "we are only here to provide value, we are not selling you anything".

**Also agreed:**
- **Cadence 7 a week.** He proposed 4, Ansh argued for 10, settled at 7 for data volume.
- **First 15 posts are explicit experiments** across formats — tweet cards, infographics, personal
  images — to find what works.
- **A separate visual identity**: new brand colours, fonts, profile picture, banner.
  "Your online identity will be far away from TLM. Connected, but TLM would be 50% by a stretch."
- **BOFU posts on demand.** He sends a voice note plus an image when TLM does something (e.g. the
  demo room launch) and we turn it into a post. He asked for this explicitly.
- **He relaxed the figures rule.** The $3M objection was only about revealing that number, not the
  angle: "if there was a different way to spin it, it's fine… they also will prefer not to do too
  much on figures."

## 7. Access

**LinkedIn credentials received on the 31 Jul call.** Username, password, and the Google
Authenticator seed key, all sent in the WhatsApp chat. Screenshot saved. Unipile link also sent.
Handle: linkedin.com/in/manishkeshwani. Email manish@tlmintl.com.

Live baseline at handover (2026-07-30): **1,256 followers, 1,293 connections, 2.5 posts a month,
median 46 reactions, 4.7% engagement, 13 of 30 posts with zero comments.** Posts with a point of
view beat announcements by 74% (54 vs 31 median). Best post ever: 175 reactions, about Ubiquiti's
CEO at UWC London.

## 8. Permanent exclusions (his section 8, standing)

His reason: "At this cadence I will not be reading every draft with fresh eyes by week six, so the
line has to hold without me."

1. Compliance, tax, regulatory, legal, entity financials — however anonymised.
   "Operator judgement, yes. Operator confessions, no."
2. **Named vendors or brands in any critical framing.** One model he describes runs at a live
   counterparty; a critical post is "the fastest way to end it".
3. Named or identifiable employees without consent.
4. Salaries, individual revenue attribution, business unit revenue.
5. Pipeline brands and forward-looking category bets. Categories in general terms are fine.
6. Precise internal timelines, comp thinking, live decisions. Broad arc public, mechanics not.
7. **No claim that TLM deliberately placed a brand into a market.** "Several of our strongest
   partnerships came to us because of presence we already had, and I will not dress that up as
   strategy I executed."

Plus: **nothing that reads as public disappointment in a named team. His HR leadership reads
LinkedIn.** And: never a post about his father or the family — write about what changes when a
business stops running on one person's relationships.

## 9. Facts, locked

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| Title | CEO, TLM Group |
| Age | 36 |
| Business age | 30 years, founded by his father |
| Headcount | 250 |
| Countries | 56 |
| Entities | 5, including 3 in West Africa |
| Interviews | close to 600 a year — do not round up, a reader divides by working days |
| Brands | 18 |
| Unverified, do not publish | 60% handshake leads, 3x close rate, 70-80 promotions, ~100 credit repeats |

## 10. Style rules he set

- No hedging. Make the claim, acknowledge the cost, never pre-apologise.
- Not every anecdote a male voice.
- No slop lines: "here is the part nobody puts on a slide" and similar.
- No sport-to-work analogies. He hates them.
- Specificity over checklists. "Hormozi is sooo specific." A signal listed without its mechanism
  is a checklist, not an insight.
- Objective brag, never pretentious brag.

Right — leverage first, then pillars. Here's the reasoning.

## What the profile can actually do for him

| Lever | Value now | Value in 5-6 years |
|---|---|---|
| **Hiring** | 80/20 modern-to-executive, senior layer over 1-3 yrs | The candidate pool compounds; he stops competing on salary |
| **Brand acquisition** | Makes the cold DM land — principals read before replying | Brands approach him instead |
| **Employer brand** | 250 staff read it; HR is his stated vehicle | Retention of the people he's betting on |
| **New verticals** | Zero reputation in robotics / AI hardware today | First-mover credibility where he has none yet |
| **His own optionality** | — | **This is the big one** |

That last row is the strategic insight, and it's his own: **he has given himself until his early forties to make himself unnecessary at TLM.** He's 36. The audience he builds now is the asset he spends then — boards, investing, the next thing, whatever it is. Nobody builds a following at 42 from a standing start. **The feed is the option he's buying on his own future.**

That reframes everything: we're not writing a distribution executive's LinkedIn. We're building the personal capital of a man who is deliberately engineering his way out of the job he holds.

## The 6 pillars

| # | Pillar | Lever it pulls | Brag level | Audience |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **The Hiring Engine** — 600 interviews/yr, what he reads in 2 minutes, hire the person not the vacancy, reassign before removing | Hiring + employer brand | Credential | Candidates, founders, HR |
| **2** | **Trust as Infrastructure** — credit with no bureau score, what you read instead of a filing, pricing for the losses, why a market isn't real until someone's stood in it | Credibility in hard markets | Scale | Operators, principals |
| **3** | **The Distributor's View** — fragmentation kills brands, geography arbitrage, what brands get wrong entering MEA | **Brand acquisition — the money pillar** | Scale / Full | Brand principals, channel directors |
| **4** | **Making Yourself Unnecessary** — second-gen, institution-building, judgement that can't be taught stops at you, auditing inherited decisions | Senior hiring + his 5-yr optionality | Full | Senior operators |
| **5** | **Borrowed Brains** — books, Paul Graham, Naval, Hoffman, Zero to One, with his take on top | Reach at scale, **needs none of his time** | Full | Broad business |
| **6** | **Sequencing New Technology** — personally maximalist, organisationally conservative. Not AI content; how a 250-person company adopts anything | Modern talent (the 80%) + new verticals | Credential / Scale | Builders, operators |

**Brag rotates across all three levels** as you said — credential on pillar 1 and 6, scale on 2 and 3, full on 4 and 5. That stops it becoming a tic and gives us data on which opener converts.

**Pillar 5 is the volume engine.** It's the only one that scales to 7 posts a week without his input, which is the entire problem you named on the call. Pillars 1-4 are his moat; pillar 5 is how we hold cadence.

## Proposed batch of 10

**Carried (4):** what I read in 2 minutes · Chesky/600 interviews · credit mechanism · automating my own job

**New (6):**
5. **Geography arbitrage** — a brand with 4 distributors in Dubai and zero in West Africa *(P3)*
6. **Fragmentation kills brands** — 2 backed properly beats 6 competing on price *(P3)*
7. **The flagship brag-listicle** — the "18 things" post you described to him *(P5)*
8. **His take on a known framework** — Blitzscaling read from a 250-person real-economy business *(P5)*
9. **Making myself unnecessary** — the institution arc *(P4)*
10. **How a 250-person company adopts anything new** — sequencing, not evangelism *(P6)*

Every pillar gets at least one post. Formats spread across tweet cards, infographics and personal images so week one still functions as the experiment he agreed to.

**Tell me which pillars you want to keep or cut and I'll build all 10 plus the new strategy deck.** My only strong view: pillar 3 is non-negotiable because it's the one that converts brands, and pillar 5 is non-negotiable because without it we can't hold 7 a week.
